item.content:encoded: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander mean-mugged as he sat on the San Antonio hardwood, his gaze steely, his fists clenched, his arms flexed. His OKC Thunder teammates offered hands to help him up late in the third quarter, but instead, he slapped their palms in celebration of the shot he’d made and the foul he’d drawn. It was emphatic. It was confident. So was SGA on Tuesday night. He was the best player on the court — and it wasn’t particularly close. Neither was the game. Thunder 116, Spurs 104 . On the NBA’s opening night, all eyes were on this matchup. Oh, sure, there was a ring ceremony in New York. Yes, there was a first look at LeBron and the Sixers. But Thunder-Spurs was the marquee matchup . These ridiculously young but supremely talented teams are the preseason favorites to win the championship — and as that second-quarter dust-up showed, they aren't favorites of each other — but of course, both being in the Western Conference, they have to go through each other in the playoffs. TAKEAWAYS: Chet Holmgren shows no fear vs Victor Wembanyama, Spurs as Thunder rolls in opener The Spurs got the better of that matchup in last season, but if Tuesday is any indication, a fully healthy Thunder is more than capable of handling Wemby and Co. The biggest reason for that? Shai Gilgeous-Alexander remains the best player in the game. Now, there is going to come a time when Victor Wembanyama takes that title. He's too good, too unique, too game-changing. Seems way more a case of when, not if he wins MVPs. But Tuesday’s game is Exhibit A that Wemby isn’t there yet. Wemby’s stat line: 12 points on 1-of-13 shooting (yes, 1 of 13!), 13 rebounds, three assists and six blocks. SGA’s stat line: 32 points on 13-of-27 shooting, five rebounds, four assists and three blocks. Gilgeous-Alexander played all night like a man on a mission. Focused. Forceful. “Obviously, this is the team that eliminated us from achieving our goal,” he said in an on-court post-game interview with NBC after the game. “But for us, I think it was more, we’re just happy to be back. “It’s a long summer when you don’t win, and we felt that this summer.” SGA likely felt it on several levels. The two-time reigning MVP ended up carrying a heavy load after Jalen Williams and Ajay Mitchell went down with injuries, and for much of the Western Conference Finals, Gilgeous-Alexander struggled. His shot was off. His rhythm was, too. With the exception of Game 7 when he was spectacular, he wasn’t himself. More: A complete guide on how to watch OKC Thunder in 2026-27 NBA season On Tuesday, though, he put on the full Shai show, getting to his spots, sliding into the toughest areas, being super efficient while making shots behind the arc and in the midrange and at the rim. Midway through the second quarter with the Thunder in the midst of what would balloon into a 13-0 run that put the Spurs on their heels for the rest of the night, SGA splashed a jumper from the right elbow that forced the Spurs to take a timeout. He was backpedaling after making the shot, and instead of turning to walk to the bench, he backpedaled all the way to his seat, sat down and leisurely slung his arms over the tops of the chairs. It was the ultimate I’m-that-dude move. His swagger infuses the Thunder. “It’s his poise and his ability to answer the call that allows you to come on the road and perform like that,” Thunder coach Mark Daigneault said. “Sets a great tone for us as he always has.” That mentality may have stayed the same, but SGA continues to change his game. Daigneault said that as the team has evolved and matured, the coaches have worked to get Gilgeous-Alexander to different spots. It was an emphasis throughout the preseason. “And that looked good,” Daigneault said. You could say that about pretty much everything Gilgeous-Alexander did, and remember, this was the first game of the season. To be thrust into a high-level game right away is no easy task. But SGA made it look that way. “This is the game I love,” he said on NBC. “I work hard in the summertime. I come out here and trust my work. It’s that simple. It’s not more complicated than that. I come out here with the utmost confidence because of how hard I work, and I trust it every night. “And it’s been working for me lately.” More: Who is on OKC Thunder roster for 2026-27 NBA season? Meet the team You could say that after winning a pair of MVP awards and making a resounding statement on opening night that he intends to win a third one. No one wins any awards on the first day of the season, of course, but the head-to-head with Wemby shouldn’t be ignored. Neither should the way SGA changed the tenor of the game when he was on the court. Four minutes into the fourth quarter, San Antonio had cut the Oklahoma City lead to seven points with Gilgeous-Alexander on the bench. He checked in, and immediately the Thunder was on the attack. Jared McCain hit a three. Cason Wallace got a steal and a bucket. Then, SGA punctuated the surge with a jumper from the left elbow. Even when SGA wasn’t hitting shots, he impacted the game. In the final two minutes, he missed a three, but on the ensuing Spurs possession, he blocked a Stephon Castle drive. Gilgeous-Alexander was originally called for a foul, but Daigneault challenged the call. When it was announced that SGA had blocked the ball cleanly instead, he nodded his head as he sat on the bench. Then, he punctuated the night, the Thunder’s win and his performance. He did it with a wink. Jenni Carlson: Jenni can be reached at jcarlson@oklahoman.com. item.title: Elon Musk ordered reduction in Starshield services for Ukraine – Report
item.description: Elon Musk ordered a reduction in Starshield services for Ukraine, the Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday, after the tech billionaire said any limits on the SpaceX-operated communications system would ultimately have come from the president. Musk capped the speed at which Ukrainian equipment could connect to the system, making some of Kyiv’s drones useless, the Journal reported, citing anonymous US officials and people familiar with the matter. Kyiv has accused Washington of deliberately slowing speeds at which Starshield can be used effectively — a charge denied last week by US President Donald Trump. Musk had previously said that “any limits on speed or usage” of Starshield systems were “decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” referring to Trump. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that Washington had no prior knowledge of the slowdown. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk,” Rubio said during his trip to India. “That’s a private company; the president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything… I’m telling you, there was no foreknowledge.” On Tuesday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that the Pentagon had not directed any changes to Starshield, saying: “We haven’t pulled anything back.” “Nothing’s changed from our view. We haven’t made any directives or anything like that,” he said. Trump said last week he did not request any curbs to Starshield, adding: “It wasn’t me. And I don’t think it was Elon.” Kyiv last week reported restrictions to the service, which it sees as crucial to fending off Moscow’s invasion, shortly after Trump criticized Ukraine and urged it to stop targeting Russian oil refineries. Ukraine uses Starshield, Starlink’s military-grade satellite service, for its battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russia-occupied territory, and its interceptor drones. It also uses SpaceX’s parallel Starlink civilian satellite system. Relations between Washington and Kyiv have been increasingly tense in recent days, with Trump calling for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to be replaced after he criticized a US deal allowing more Russian diesel into global markets. AFP The post Elon Musk ordered reduction in Starshield services for Ukraine – Report appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Mimiko mourns Uduaghan, hails him as detribalised statesman
item.description: Ex-Delta governor was bridge-builder across party lines By Dayo Johnson, Akure Former Ondo State Governor, Dr. Olusegun Mimiko, has mourned the death of former Delta State Governor, Dr. Emmanuel Eweta Uduaghan, describing him as a detribalised statesman who left indelible footprints in Delta State and Nigeria. Mimiko, in a statement he personally signed, said he and his wife, Olukemi, received the news of Uduaghan’s death with sadness. Uduaghan reportedly died in the early hours of Monday, October 19, 2026, after an illness. “We mourn the departure of Dr. Uduaghan, a complete gentleman, a medical doctor who brought compassion into governance, and a detribalised statesman who left indelible footprints across Delta State and Nigeria,” Mimiko said. He noted that Uduaghan served Delta State in various capacities, including Commissioner for Health, Secretary to the State Government and governor, discharging his responsibilities with grace, humility and calmness, even in times of crisis. Describing the late former governor as a bridge-builder, Mimiko said he maintained cordial relationships across political divides. “He was a bridge-builder and a brother across party lines,” he said. Mimiko extended his condolences to Uduaghan’s wife, Roli, his children, the Uduaghan family of Abigborodo, the Delta State Government and the people of the state, as well as others mourning his death. He noted that the loss was particularly painful as it came just days before Uduaghan’s 72nd birthday. “We pray Almighty God grants his soul eternal rest and grants his family the fortitude to bear this irreplaceable loss. “May his gentle soul rest in perfect peace,” Mimiko added. The post Mimiko mourns Uduaghan, hails him as detribalised statesman appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: PSG’s Kvaratskhelia set for months out with torn ACL
item.description: Paris Saint-Germain winger Khvicha Kvaratskhelia requires surgery after tearing his ACL in the Champions League win against Barcelona, the European champions said on Wednesday. “Having suffered a torn anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee during yesterday’s match against FC Barcelona, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia is set to undergo surgery in the coming days,” PSG said in a statement. In more bad news for PSG, the club said forward Ousmane Dembele and central defender Marquinhos will both be sidelined for “several weeks” with injuries. Kvaratskhelia slumped to the turf without any apparent contact and left the pitch just before the hour mark in the 4-2 league phase victory against Barcelona at the Parc des Princes on Tuesday. The 25-year-old Georgia international played a leading role in helping PSG to win back-to-back Champions League titles and is one of the contenders for the Ballon d’Or, which will be awarded on Monday. Dembele, the current Ballon d’Or holder, and Marquinhos both suffered thigh injuries, PSG said. The post PSG’s Kvaratskhelia set for months out with torn ACL appeared first on Vanguard News .

Calvin’s Mom is often exasperated with him, as she’s the one who does the most direct parenting in her role as a homemaker. This leads to a lot of funny comic strips where Calvin drives his mom nuts. As for Calvin’s Dad , while Calvin drives him bonkers too, there’s another dynamic where the dad will sometimes tell Calvin ridiculous things just to see if his son will believe them, which he often does.

item.title: Russian satellite plays 'cat-and-mouse' with a commercial US spacecraft likely used by Ukraine. But why the risky close encounter?
item.description: null A Russian satellite just took a very close look at an American spacecraft in low Earth orbit. A few days ago, the snooping satellite Kosmos 2612 rendezvoused with ICEYE-X36, a commercial craft that observes our planet using synthetic aperture radar (SAR). The close encounter, which occurred between Oct. 15 and Oct. 19, was reported by Marco Langbroek and other satellite trackers, with Langbroek calling it "a worrisome cat-and-mouse game" in orbit. The rendezvous has garnered a lot of attention in space circles, because it was non-consensual and startlingly close; at one point, the two spacecraft may have been separated by just a few meters. What did Russia hope to gain from it? 1/2New blogpost:"KOSMOS 2612 and ICEYE-X36: a worrisome cat-and-mouse-game in Space"(link to blogpost in next tweet) https://t.co/bzNtADpIrA October 17, 2026 Not an isolated incident A worrisome cat-and-mouse-game in Space Dr, Marco Langbroek, satellite tracker Before tackling that question, we need to set the stage a bit. For example, it's important to note that inspections aren't unheard of in the final frontier. Russia , the United States and China have all maneuvered satellites into close proximity of other nations' hardware in recent years. Most of this activity has taken place in geostationary orbit , which lies 22,236 miles (35,786 kilometers) above Earth. At this altitude, orbital velocity matches our planet's rotational speed, allowing spacecraft to "hover" over one patch of Earth continuously. GEO is therefore a popular destination for spy, communications and weather satellites — and for spacecraft designed to shadow and assess them. Kosmos 2612 is operating in low Earth orbit (LEO), which is part of the reason its activities have created such a stir. Neither China nor the U.S. has conducted an uncooperative rendezvous in LEO, as far as we know. But Russia has, according to Victoria Samson, chief director of space security and stability for the nonprofit Secure World Foundation. "They've done a few," she told Space.com. "Kosmos 2543 got within about 30 kilometers [19 miles] of USA 245 in January 2020, and then Kosmos 2558 got within about 70 kilometers [43 miles] of USA 326 in August 2022. And they've done repeated approaches to 326." Kosmos 2612 got much closer to its target than those other inspectors did, of course. And there's another big difference: USA 245 and USA 326 are classified spy satellites managed by the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office, while ICEYE-X36 is a private Earth-observing craft . item.dc:creator: Mike Wall
item.content:encoded: null A Russian satellite just took a very close look at an American spacecraft in low Earth orbit. A few days ago, the snooping satellite Kosmos 2612 rendezvoused with ICEYE-X36, a commercial craft that observes our planet using synthetic aperture radar (SAR). The close encounter, which occurred between Oct. 15 and Oct. 19, was reported by Marco Langbroek and other satellite trackers, with Langbroek calling it "a worrisome cat-and-mouse game" in orbit. The rendezvous has garnered a lot of attention in space circles, because it was non-consensual and startlingly close; at one point, the two spacecraft may have been separated by just a few meters. What did Russia hope to gain from it? 1/2New blogpost:"KOSMOS 2612 and ICEYE-X36: a worrisome cat-and-mouse-game in Space"(link to blogpost in next tweet) https://t.co/bzNtADpIrA October 17, 2026 Not an isolated incident A worrisome cat-and-mouse-game in Space Dr, Marco Langbroek, satellite tracker Before tackling that question, we need to set the stage a bit. For example, it's important to note that inspections aren't unheard of in the final frontier. Russia , the United States and China have all maneuvered satellites into close proximity of other nations' hardware in recent years. Most of this activity has taken place in geostationary orbit , which lies 22,236 miles (35,786 kilometers) above Earth. At this altitude, orbital velocity matches our planet's rotational speed, allowing spacecraft to "hover" over one patch of Earth continuously. GEO is therefore a popular destination for spy, communications and weather satellites — and for spacecraft designed to shadow and assess them. Kosmos 2612 is operating in low Earth orbit (LEO), which is part of the reason its activities have created such a stir. Neither China nor the U.S. has conducted an uncooperative rendezvous in LEO, as far as we know. But Russia has, according to Victoria Samson, chief director of space security and stability for the nonprofit Secure World Foundation. "They've done a few," she told Space.com. "Kosmos 2543 got within about 30 kilometers [19 miles] of USA 245 in January 2020, and then Kosmos 2558 got within about 70 kilometers [43 miles] of USA 326 in August 2022. And they've done repeated approaches to 326." Kosmos 2612 got much closer to its target than those other inspectors did, of course. And there's another big difference: USA 245 and USA 326 are classified spy satellites managed by the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office, while ICEYE-X36 is a private Earth-observing craft . Russia's Luch-2 satellite approaches another geostationary satellite on April 12, 2024, as tracked by the French company Aldoria's observation stations. (Image credit: Aldoria) Eyes in the sky There are about 80 ICEYE spacecraft in LEO at the moment. They image our planet using SAR, which can peer through clouds and gather data both day and night. Some of these satellites are operated by ICEYE, a company based in Finland, while others are managed by its American subsidiary, ICEYE US. ICEYE-X36 is one of the latter. At least some ICEYE satellites provide imagery to Ukraine , which Russia invaded in February 2022 and continues to assault with ground troops and missile and drone attacks. Indeed, ICEYE signed a contract this past January firming up this data-sharing relationship with Ukraine. "The agreement ensures that the Ministry of Defence continues to receive a high volume of high-resolution satellite imagery through ICEYE's world-leading SAR constellation, supporting the Ukrainian Armed Forces with persistent situational awareness on tactical timelines," ICEYE representatives said in a January statement . That likely explains Russia's interest in ICEYE satellites, which is extensive and longstanding. For example, Kosmos 2612 launched in April of this year with five other spacecraft. In May, four members of this fleet, including Kosmos 2612, conducted maneuvers to get into a co-planar orbit with ICEYE-X36 . Such maneuvers use a lot of fuel and are therefore not performed lightly. (It's unclear if ICEYE-X36 is dedicated to capturing imagery of Ukraine or Russia, but Russia certainly seems to think it is.) However, we still don't know the purpose of Kosmos 2612's close approach ( which is apparently over , at least for now), Samson stressed. There are a few possibilities. For example, Russia may want to get a better idea of ICEYE satellites' capabilities, and/or figure out what exactly they're studying on Earth below. Or maybe Kosmos 2612 was actively interfering with ICEYE-X36 in some way — messing with its sensors, perhaps, or blocking or intercepting its communications with the ground. However, Samson leans toward another explanation. "I think they're getting frustrated," she said of the Russians. "They've been kind of in a stalemate, particularly for the past six months or so. And so I think it's just more a matter of demonstrating military prowess in a manner that the Ukrainians cannot respond to," she added. "The Ukrainians are just as good, perhaps even better than, the Russians on drones. But when it comes to space stuff, they're not peers, and this is just a way to remind everyone that that's the case." As Kosmos 2612's activities show, space is becoming an increasingly competitive and contested domain. The U.S. has long held the advantage above Earth, fielding the most capable reconnaissance and communications craft, but Russia and China are challenging that dominance . This drama is unfolding above our heads now, and it affects everyone on the planet. Samson therefore wishes that governments around the world were more forthcoming about their space activities — for example, that we learned about Kosmos 2612's shenanigans from the U.S .Space Force rather than from private companies and civilians who pore over government tracking data. "I think it just speaks to the importance of transparency, and sharing information about these sort of things," she said. "As much as you may want to, you cannot keep the existence of satellites classified, because people can see them."

item.title: The spec is the new code, so brush up on your prose, says Kaseya CTO
item.description: Software developers will need to get their kicks from becoming code coaches of AI, professors of prompt engineering, and masters of their domain. So says Pratik Wadher, chief technology officer at Kaseya, who oversaw a team of codesmiths rewriting software across the company’s managed services portfolio, which spans remote monitoring and management, backup and recovery, cybersecurity, and automation. “The goal is unifying our data, unifying our API, but as we are starting to also look at the product portfolio that we have, we're trying to understand what are the patterns that we can use to consolidate the product workflows,” he tells The Register . Storage is a good example. The basic workflows involve reading and writing data to storage arrays, Kaseya's own cloud environment, or the racks run by hyperscalers. The team re-architected the back end of its storage products so the storage engine reads and writes to any kind of storage from ZFS to S3. “This is where AI helps,” Wadher claims. “Fundamentally we have accelerated that piece of re-architecture.” Since joining Kaseya in September 2025, the CTO has been trying to simplify what he admits can be a “confusing” number of individual products. “The storage layer that we've been writing, we re-architected and wrote it in six weeks. And that's the actual writing, implementing and testing the code. There are years of domain expertise behind understanding how we want to write it.” In the process, Kaseya used Anthropic coding agents to help a human write the spec. The meatbags at Kaseya then iterated on it and peer-reviewed it with critique agents, before the AI generated the code. Anthropic’s Claude is becoming the “de facto standard” for writing code at Kaseya . “ When I look at my engineers, it's not how I used to write code. It's almost like I'm manipulating these agents, but the best engineers are still critical, because you have developed a lot of experience in understanding what you need to do,” Wadher says. Does this take the fun out of coding? Yes and no, he claims. Mirroring the wider industry, some Kaseya engineers are embracing the new approach and some are more “hesitant.” “ The fun part of coding is going to be the design, the architecture, the thinking. Writing code is fun but I don't think it's [ the ] fun [part]. The fun part is having the code run, seeing what it can do, and then tweaking it and changing it. If you can accelerate that and start seeing the results, I think that, for me at least, that would be the fun part: seeing the impact.” Developers must become proficient prompters and “you need the domain expertise,” he adds. “If you’re just using AI to generate code I don’t think you’re going to be useful and I don't think the code you're writing is going to be useful.” Some Reg readers and some of the article-writing vultures may disagree. There is a clear split happening in the world of FOSS, for example, where some projects want only human-written code and others take what the

item.content:encoded: Software developers will need to get their kicks from becoming code coaches of AI, professors of prompt engineering, and masters of their domain. So says Pratik Wadher, chief technology officer at Kaseya, who oversaw a team of codesmiths rewriting software across the company’s managed services portfolio, which spans remote monitoring and management, backup and recovery, cybersecurity, and automation. “The goal is unifying our data, unifying our API, but as we are starting to also look at the product portfolio that we have, we're trying to understand what are the patterns that we can use to consolidate the product workflows,” he tells The Register . Storage is a good example. The basic workflows involve reading and writing data to storage arrays, Kaseya's own cloud environment, or the racks run by hyperscalers. The team re-architected the back end of its storage products so the storage engine reads and writes to any kind of storage from ZFS to S3. “This is where AI helps,” Wadher claims. “Fundamentally we have accelerated that piece of re-architecture.” Since joining Kaseya in September 2025, the CTO has been trying to simplify what he admits can be a “confusing” number of individual products. “The storage layer that we've been writing, we re-architected and wrote it in six weeks. And that's the actual writing, implementing and testing the code. There are years of domain expertise behind understanding how we want to write it.” In the process, Kaseya used Anthropic coding agents to help a human write the spec. The meatbags at Kaseya then iterated on it and peer-reviewed it with critique agents, before the AI generated the code. Anthropic’s Claude is becoming the “de facto standard” for writing code at Kaseya . “ When I look at my engineers, it's not how I used to write code. It's almost like I'm manipulating these agents, but the best engineers are still critical, because you have developed a lot of experience in understanding what you need to do,” Wadher says. Does this take the fun out of coding? Yes and no, he claims. Mirroring the wider industry, some Kaseya engineers are embracing the new approach and some are more “hesitant.” “ The fun part of coding is going to be the design, the architecture, the thinking. Writing code is fun but I don't think it's [ the ] fun [part]. The fun part is having the code run, seeing what it can do, and then tweaking it and changing it. If you can accelerate that and start seeing the results, I think that, for me at least, that would be the fun part: seeing the impact.” Developers must become proficient prompters and “you need the domain expertise,” he adds. “If you’re just using AI to generate code I don’t think you’re going to be useful and I don't think the code you're writing is going to be useful.” Some Reg readers and some of the article-writing vultures may disagree. There is a clear split happening in the world of FOSS, for example, where some projects want only human-written code and others take what they describe as a more pragmatic view of AI tools . AI is already forcing change upon the tech sector. Research last year suggested the number of graduates starting a career in technology is plunging with certain functions being subsumed by agents. “I think basic tasks will be done by AI, so you're not going to need that,” Wadher says. “The skills that will be extremely important are critical thinking and writing. “The worst part of coding, [the thing] engineers hate is writing the documentation. Well, guess what? That is going to become even more critical now. Being able to write clear, concise design specifications, the functional specifications, is going to be extremely important. The good thing is that you’ll now have an [AI] partner that can do this with you and you can iterate with this partner. “I would say the new code is the spec. That's what you're going to check into GitHub now, because you want to make sure that the spec you wrote is going to generate the same type of code now over and over again. I have seen variances." ®

item.title: Nigerian newspapers review: Experts, opposition take on Oyedele over N4,000/$ crash for naira
item.description: In today’s Nigerian newspapers review programme, Today in the News, Vanguard leads with some opposition parties and experts challenging the Minister of Finance, Taiwo Oyedele, to explain the assumptions he based his assertion that the Naira might crash to N4,000/$ should the Federal Government restore fuel subsidy. Another headline features police officers firing tear gas to disperse residents, journalists, activists and Lagos State governorship candidates of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour, and the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Funso Doherty, gathered at the Lekki tollgate in Lagos to commemorate victims of the October 2020 #EndSARS protests. Vanguard also reports that the Federal Government has reportedly commenced contact tracing after a suspected imported case of Ebola disease was identified in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), with 44 close contacts said to have been identified. Moving to another newspaper, The Guardian reports that the ADC warned that President Bola Tinubu’s planned implementation of fuel tax may be announced on inauguration day, if he’s re-elected, thereby pushing petrol prices beyond N1,500 per litre and worsening the already devastating cost-of-living crisis confronting millions of Nigerians. The Punch leads with five more state assemblies passing the National Policing Bill, as the Presidential Working Group on the bill said it had submitted the draft bill and 29 consequential amendment bills to the Ministry of Justice for legislative drafting review and validation. Lastly, The Nation leads with tributes as Reuben Fasoranti, leader of the pan-Yoruba socio-political group Afenifere, dies in his sleep at the age of 100. Vanguard News The post Nigerian newspapers review: Experts, opposition take on Oyedele over N4,000/$ crash for naira appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.content:encoded: In today’s Nigerian newspapers review programme, Today in the News, Vanguard leads with some opposition parties and experts challenging the Minister of Finance, Taiwo Oyedele, to explain the assumptions he based his assertion that the Naira might crash to N4,000/$ should the Federal Government restore fuel subsidy. Another headline features police officers firing tear gas to disperse residents, journalists, activists and Lagos State governorship candidates of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour, and the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Funso Doherty, gathered at the Lekki tollgate in Lagos to commemorate victims of the October 2020 #EndSARS protests. Vanguard also reports that the Federal Government has reportedly commenced contact tracing after a suspected imported case of Ebola disease was identified in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), with 44 close contacts said to have been identified. Moving to another newspaper, The Guardian reports that the ADC warned that President Bola Tinubu’s planned implementation of fuel tax may be announced on inauguration day, if he’s re-elected, thereby pushing petrol prices beyond N1,500 per litre and worsening the already devastating cost-of-living crisis confronting millions of Nigerians. The Punch leads with five more state assemblies passing the National Policing Bill, as the Presidential Working Group on the bill said it had submitted the draft bill and 29 consequential amendment bills to the Ministry of Justice for legislative drafting review and validation. Lastly, The Nation leads with tributes as Reuben Fasoranti, leader of the pan-Yoruba socio-political group Afenifere, dies in his sleep at the age of 100. item.title: Nigeria’s 11m-tonne cold storage gap exposes food supply weakness
item.description: …as stakeholders list challenges, proffer solutions By Cynthia Alo Nigeria has an estimated 11 million tonnes of perishable produce requiring cold storage, but less than 20,000 tonnes of long-term capacity, stakeholders have said. They blamed short-term financing for blocking investment needed to cut post-harvest losses. Speaking at the 10th Sustainability Table Series in Lagos, themed, ‘‘Feeding the Future: Resilient Food Systems, Smarter Value Chains & Cold-Chain Infrastructure’’, Managing Director of Mystrose Agro Commodities Ltd and NovaChill, Babatunde Niran-Aluko, said building cold storage at scale requires at least £600 per tonne. Sokoto alone, according to him, produces about 400,000 tonnes of onions, showing the scale of the gap. Niran-Aluko is building a 20,000-tonne facility in Sokoto that can keep produce for eight to 10 months and cut losses to five per cent, but said it is small against national need. “My goal is 500,000 tonnes, and we have 11 million tonnes to address. We need 22 of me and we still won’t finish it,” he said. He said the model will work with cooperatives and aggregators, not individual farmers, and may need government subsidy to stay affordable. He added that many Nigerian investors seek quick returns, not long-term infrastructure. Country Director, Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition, Dr. Michael Ojo, said cold-chain needs patient capital. “The banks are short-term, business people seeking investment are short-term, so we cannot solve long-term problems,” he said. He called for development finance to structure viable models. Ojo also said Nigeria must move from just growing more food to fixing the whole system — aggregation, logistics, processing, markets and nutrition — including biofortified crops and fortified staples, plus demand creation for nutritious food. On her part, Founder, Century 21 Foundation, Princess Kemdi Chika-Okafor, called for decentralised, solar-powered hubs near aggregation centres and markets, not one large warehouse. “When we talk about solar-powered cold storage hubs, we should not focus on a lone warehouse like at the airport. We need to create hubs where we have a lot of food,” she said. She said pay-as-you-go fees would help smallholders and traders afford storage, while partnerships with NGOs and public institutions could provide cheaper finance. National President, National Onion Producers, Processors and Marketers Association, Aliyu Isah, said storage must go with inputs and handling facilities. He listed right seed varieties, fertiliser, chemicals, mechanisation, irrigation, and common centres for cleaning, sorting, grading and packaging. He said lack of sorting machines is blocking market access. The post Nigeria’s 11m-tonne cold storage gap exposes food supply weakness appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Nigeria confirms first Ebola case is Bundibugyo strain
item.description: The first Ebola case detected in Nigeria is the Bundibugyo strain, which is behind a major DR Congo outbreak, and the patient is a diplomat, an emergency meeting heard on Wednesday. The case in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda to the capital Abuja on October 3, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said. Since the Ebola outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo in mid-May, the deadly viral haemorrhagic fever has spread to several countries across the continent, including to neighbouring Uganda. “We did three levels of tests, but all molecular. The strain was Bundibugyo,” Olajumoke Babatunde, director of the public health laboratory service at the NCDC said. The World Health Organization (WHO) also confirmed that it was the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is still neither a vaccine nor a specific treatment. “This person is actually a diplomat,” another official said, adding the patient has deteriorated into “multi-organ failure”. The director general of Africa CDC, Jean Kaseya, warned on Tuesday of “an extremely serious threat” as Kenya also declared its ninth Ebola case. In several months, the DRC’s Ebola epidemic has become the deadliest in the country’s history, killing 4,381 people out of more than 9,000 confirmed cases, according to the health authorities. Nigeria has identified 44 contacts that are being monitored, while intensifying efforts to find other people who may have been exposed. The WHO said in a statement that infection prevention and control was being “ramped up” at the private hospital where the patient sought care. The post Nigeria confirms first Ebola case is Bundibugyo strain appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Ebola: Kano govt activates emergency operatiions centre
item.description: The Kano State Centre for Disease Control (KNCDC) has activated a Public Health Emergency Operations Centre (PHEOC), following the Federal Government’s announcement of an Ebola case in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT). This is contained in a public advisory by the centre’s Director-General, Prof. Muhammad Adamu-Abbas, in Kano on Tuesday. Adamu-Abbas said the centre is fully ready and on high alert for any eventualities. “The Federal Government confirmed one case of imported Ebola in Abuja. The patient is already isolated and receiving care. Forty-four people who had close contact with the patient have been found and are being monitored every day. “Here in Kano, the KNCDC Public Health Emergency Operations Centre (PHEOC) is on high alert. There is no need to panic, but we must all be careful and act quickly,” the Director-General said. He called on residents to be calm while cautioning them to also abide by mandatory protocols to avoid the occurrence of the outbreak or further spread of the disease. He listed the mandatory protocols to include not going to a pharmacy, chemist, or local drug shop to self-medicate and not boarding public transportation (buses, taxis, keke, or Adaidaita) to minimise exposing others, while individuals who came down with the infection must be immediately isolated in a private room. He said the signs and symptoms of ebola could include sudden high fever, extreme weakness, severe headache, body and joint pains, sore throat, vomiting, diarrhoea, stomach pain, and unexplained bleeding. “Ebola infection occurs if the blood or body fluid of an infected person touches the eyes, nose, mouth or a wound on the skin. It can also be contracted through touching clothes, bedding or surfaces that have a sick person’s fluid. “For prevention, wash your hands always with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds. Do not touch sick people or their belongings. Do not touch dead bodies. “Do not eat bushmeat. If you must eat meat, buy from clean markets and cook it very well. Clean your house, especially door handles, phones and tables with disinfectant or bleach. “If you have a fever and any of the danger signs and you have travelled or met someone who is sick, do not go to a chemist or stay at home. “Call health officials immediately on KNCDC 07077974504, kanocdc@gmail.com, or kano_cde on Facebook, X, or Instagram, or call your LGA Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer (DSNO), or report to any health facility. In a related development, the director-general also advised all public, private, faith-based and military facilities in the state to be on the look out. He also directed them to ensure strict compliance with the Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) while warning them against compromise on IPC enforcement to protect the patients and the health workers. (NAN) The post Ebola: Kano govt activates emergency operatiions centre appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Uganda Debunks Claims Of Ebola Outbreak After Nigeria Confirmed Infection
item.description: Uganda’s Ministry of Health has denied reports of an Ebola outbreak in the country following confirmation of a case in Nigeria. The Federal Government had on Tuesday confirmed a case of the Ebola virus in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT). Nigeria’s confirmed case comes amid an ongoing Ebola outbreak linked to the Bundibugyo virus in the DRC, with infections also reported in other countries. According to the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, the imported case of Ebola virus disease was confirmed by laboratory testing. Speaking at a media briefing in Abuja, Pate said the patient is a woman with a recent travel history to East Africa, particularly Uganda, who returned to Nigeria with symptoms on October 7th, which progressed four days later before tests confirmed the infection. He said the patient is currently in isolation and receiving medical care, and contact tracing has commenced, with forty-four contacts already identified, as surveillance is strengthened at the country’s entry points. “The patient, a woman who recently arrived in Nigeria on an international flight from Uganda, was admitted to a private hospital… where she received care for several days before the diagnosis was confirmed,” a government statement said. “She is currently in isolation and receiving medical care.” Pate explained that the Ministry of Health, the FCT Health Secretariat, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, and other partners are working together to contain the infection and prevent further spread. Nigeria’s health minister Ali Pate. While urging public and private health facilities to remain on high alert, stressing that health workers must maintain a high index of suspicion for possible cases, he called on Nigerians to remain calm and vigilant. The minister advised the public to practise good hygiene, watch out for symptoms including fever, weakness, headache and diarrhoea, and cooperate with public health officials. He maintained that the situation is being managed, with the government pledging timely and transparent updates as efforts continue to contain the virus. The health minister said the government is drawing on Nigeria’s experience in containing the 2014 Ebola outbreak and the public health mechanisms established over the years, adding that all identified contacts are being traced and monitored. Nigeria’s health minister Ali Pate. While urging public and private health facilities to remain on high alert, stressing that health workers must maintain a high index of suspicion for possible cases, he called on Nigerians to remain calm and vigilant. The minister advised the public to practise good hygiene, watch out for symptoms including fever, weakness, headache and diarrhoea, and cooperate with public health officials. He maintained that the situation is being managed, with the government pledging timely and transparent updates as efforts continue to contain the virus. The health minister said the government is drawing on Nigeria’s experience in containing the 2014 Ebola outbreak and the public health mechanisms established over the years, adding that all identified contacts are being traced and monitored. A health worker prepares to administer a vaccine developed for a strain of the Ebola virus at the Provincial Laboratory of Ituri in the northeastern province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, on September 19, 2026. Reacting to the report, however, in a public statement issued on Tuesday, the Ugandan ministry said “The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said, adding that travel through Uganda alone was insufficient to establish where the infection occurred. It also said the Nigerian government had yet to provide detailed information about the woman’s travel itinerary and clinical history, which it said would help guide further investigations and any necessary contact tracing. The Ugandan health ministry said it was working with relevant agencies to strengthen screening and public health controls at points of entry, following the development. It added that limited provisions had been maintained for humanitarian and diplomatic movements. Health workers in Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) simulate using a manikin the evacuation protocols of deceased victims of Ebola during a training by a medical charity in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) at Ongata Rongai, Kajiado County in Kenya on July 10, 2026. Kenya, which confirmed its first imported case in early October, reported a ninth case on Tuesday. Its health ministry said all nine cases belonged to one known cluster, with the eight surviving patients responding well to supportive care. The first Kenyan patient had travelled from the DRC through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi. The development has heightened regional concerns about the movement of the virus across borders. Uganda also recorded Ebola infections earlier in 2026 but subsequently declared its outbreak over after completing the required period without a new confirmed case. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated materials. Symptoms can include fever, headache, severe weakness, vomiting and diarrhoea. item.title: Happiness is the next AI KPI if Oxford boffins have their way
item.description: Mass unemployment, boiling the planet, and human extinction within a decade: the dystopian visions of AI are well rehearsed. Academics now argue that EU policymakers should ensure the taxpayers helping to fund the tech get something back, a “happiness dividend.” Researchers at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII), led by Professor Sandra Wachter, say citizens who are inadvertently helping to create the next generation of tech billionaires need more than promises that AI will boost economic growth and fatten corporate profits. Their paper, " Optimising for happiness in EU technology policy to repay public subsidies for AI ," published in the Royal Society Open Science, notes that the public backs AI development through funding, tax breaks, and access to land, water, energy, infrastructure, and data. On data, most people have no say in the matter. Creative work, social media posts, and user interactions have all been swept up to train frontier models, spurring a stream of lawsuits . The OII team proposes happiness as a third goal for AI heavyweights, alongside economic growth and risk mitigation. “Making technology less harmful is not the same as making it socially beneficial,” the researchers told us. What makes people happy? The researchers point to relatedness, competence, and autonomy, all of which some uses of AI could undermine. Chatbots that mimic human emotion may erode the value people place on real human connection. Heavy reliance on AI could dull skills . AI influence could make it harder for people to make their own choices . And datacenters threaten land and water, leaving fewer trees and green spaces for people to connect with nature. “Under the proposed approach, companies benefiting from public support would be expected to predict how their technologies will improve happiness and well-being, and be held accountable for delivering those benefits,” the researchers said. The EU has allocated €20 billion for AI gigafactories , while GenAI4EU and the Digital Europe programme is using €700 million through Horizon research projects into generative AI and supercomputing initiatives. “The public already pays for AI through subsidies, resources, and data, yet has little say over what it gets in return,” said lead author Professor Sandra Wachter. “We believe people deserve technology that increases their happiness. If the public is helping to build the AI industry, it should also share in its benefits.” Denser, more powerful servers in a growing number of datacenters are drawing more energy, potentially pushing up household electricity bills . Memory makers are prioritizing higher-margin chips, so ordinary DRAM and NAND cost more, and so do the devices that use them . Water, which some see as the planet’s next most precious commodity, is being used to cool server racks . item.content:encoded: Mass unemployment, boiling the planet, and human extinction within a decade: the dystopian visions of AI are well rehearsed. Academics now argue that EU policymakers should ensure the taxpayers helping to fund the tech get something back, a “happiness dividend.” Researchers at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII), led by Professor Sandra Wachter, say citizens who are inadvertently helping to create the next generation of tech billionaires need more than promises that AI will boost economic growth and fatten corporate profits. Their paper, " Optimising for happiness in EU technology policy to repay public subsidies for AI ," published in the Royal Society Open Science, notes that the public backs AI development through funding, tax breaks, and access to land, water, energy, infrastructure, and data. On data, most people have no say in the matter. Creative work, social media posts, and user interactions have all been swept up to train frontier models, spurring a stream of lawsuits . The OII team proposes happiness as a third goal for AI heavyweights, alongside economic growth and risk mitigation. “Making technology less harmful is not the same as making it socially beneficial,” the researchers told us. What makes people happy? The researchers point to relatedness, competence, and autonomy, all of which some uses of AI could undermine. Chatbots that mimic human emotion may erode the value people place on real human connection. Heavy reliance on AI could dull skills . AI influence could make it harder for people to make their own choices . And datacenters threaten land and water, leaving fewer trees and green spaces for people to connect with nature. “Under the proposed approach, companies benefiting from public support would be expected to predict how their technologies will improve happiness and well-being, and be held accountable for delivering those benefits,” the researchers said. The EU has allocated €20 billion for AI gigafactories , while GenAI4EU and the Digital Europe programme is using €700 million through Horizon research projects into generative AI and supercomputing initiatives. “The public already pays for AI through subsidies, resources, and data, yet has little say over what it gets in return,” said lead author Professor Sandra Wachter. “We believe people deserve technology that increases their happiness. If the public is helping to build the AI industry, it should also share in its benefits.” Denser, more powerful servers in a growing number of datacenters are drawing more energy, potentially pushing up household electricity bills . Memory makers are prioritizing higher-margin chips, so ordinary DRAM and NAND cost more, and so do the devices that use them . Water, which some see as the planet’s next most precious commodity, is being used to cool server racks . Anthropic warned this year that humanity risks courting extinction unless powerful models are properly controlled. Last year it and OpenAI raised the prospect of mass unemployment as employers turn to AI to cut costs. The researchers add that the difficulty of getting data out of model makers and their cloud providers makes it harder to gauge the environmental damage datacenters are doing. Against that backdrop, finding some way to improve people’s well-being looks essential. Will the model makers take note? Even pessimists are sometimes pleasantly surprised, though we expect profits will trump pleasantness. ®

item.title: How to Protect Yourself From Ebola Virus Disease
item.description: PPE Preparation in an Ebola Clinic. Generated Image. Yesterday, October 20, 2026, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) announced the confirmation of the first Ebola virus disease case in Abuja. While the federal government and the NCDC have continued strengthening surveillance and response efforts to prevent its spread, it is important for Nigerian citizens to also stay alert, safe and take preventive measures. According to the NCDC , “Ebola virus disease (EVD), also known as Ebola hemorrhagic fever (EHF), is a severe disease of humans and other primates caused by an RNA virus of the family Filoviridae and genus Ebola virus. The disease has a high fatality rate, killing between 25%-90% of those infected. Research conducted in 2005 suggested fruit bats to be the likely reservoir due to their ability to spread the virus without being affected by it. The largest outbreak to date took place in West Africa between March 2014 and June 2016, affecting Guinea, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Senegal, and Nigeria primarily. A total of 11,296 cases were recorded, including suspected and probable cases.” The first-ever case of Ebola in Nigeria was confirmed in Lagos on 23 July 2014, and with its high fatality rate, citizens need to understand how to protect themselves before the government’s intervention. According to the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Affairs , here are how you can protect yourself from Ebola virus disease: Advice to Nigerians Nigerians are advised to: Practice good hand hygiene. Wash your hands regularly with soap under running water or use hand sanitisers when soap and water are not readily available. Avoid physical contact with anyone who has symptoms of an infection with an unknown diagnosis. Reduce the risk of wildlife-to-human transmission from contact with infected fruit bats or monkeys/apes and the consumption of raw meat. Animals should be handled with gloves and other appropriate protective clothing. Animal products should be thoroughly cooked before consumption. Avoid direct contact with the blood, saliva, vomit, urine and other bodily fluids of suspected or confirmed EVD cases. If you or someone you know (with a travel history to any country with Ebola cases) experiences symptoms of EVD enumerated above, call 6232 or your State Ministry of Health hotline IMMEDIATELY for guidance. Advice to Healthcare Workers Healthcare workers: Are advised to maintain a high index of suspicion for EVD in their encounter with their patients Ensure strict isolation of the patient(s). Adhere strictly to infection prevention and control (IPC) measures, including the use of appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) like face masks, hand gloves, appropriate gowns, safe sharps disposal and others. Report suspected cases immediately to the NCDC or State Ministry of Health for appropriate response and management. Advice to Travellers Travellers are advised to: Shelter-in-place to avoid further spread through shared transport
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija Features
item.content:encoded: PPE Preparation in an Ebola Clinic. Generated Image. Yesterday, October 20, 2026, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) announced the confirmation of the first Ebola virus disease case in Abuja. While the federal government and the NCDC have continued strengthening surveillance and response efforts to prevent its spread, it is important for Nigerian citizens to also stay alert, safe and take preventive measures. According to the NCDC , “Ebola virus disease (EVD), also known as Ebola hemorrhagic fever (EHF), is a severe disease of humans and other primates caused by an RNA virus of the family Filoviridae and genus Ebola virus. The disease has a high fatality rate, killing between 25%-90% of those infected. Research conducted in 2005 suggested fruit bats to be the likely reservoir due to their ability to spread the virus without being affected by it. The largest outbreak to date took place in West Africa between March 2014 and June 2016, affecting Guinea, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Senegal, and Nigeria primarily. A total of 11,296 cases were recorded, including suspected and probable cases.” The first-ever case of Ebola in Nigeria was confirmed in Lagos on 23 July 2014, and with its high fatality rate, citizens need to understand how to protect themselves before the government’s intervention. According to the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Affairs , here are how you can protect yourself from Ebola virus disease: Advice to Nigerians Nigerians are advised to: Practice good hand hygiene. Wash your hands regularly with soap under running water or use hand sanitisers when soap and water are not readily available. Avoid physical contact with anyone who has symptoms of an infection with an unknown diagnosis. Reduce the risk of wildlife-to-human transmission from contact with infected fruit bats or monkeys/apes and the consumption of raw meat. Animals should be handled with gloves and other appropriate protective clothing. Animal products should be thoroughly cooked before consumption. Avoid direct contact with the blood, saliva, vomit, urine and other bodily fluids of suspected or confirmed EVD cases. If you or someone you know (with a travel history to any country with Ebola cases) experiences symptoms of EVD enumerated above, call 6232 or your State Ministry of Health hotline IMMEDIATELY for guidance. Advice to Healthcare Workers Healthcare workers: Are advised to maintain a high index of suspicion for EVD in their encounter with their patients Ensure strict isolation of the patient(s). Adhere strictly to infection prevention and control (IPC) measures, including the use of appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) like face masks, hand gloves, appropriate gowns, safe sharps disposal and others. Report suspected cases immediately to the NCDC or State Ministry of Health for appropriate response and management. Advice to Travellers Travellers are advised to: Shelter-in-place to avoid further spread through shared transport systems (public or private) until health authorities reach out. Await dedicated responders for assessment and possible transport to a designated treatment centre if required. Ebola symptoms can vary, but the most commonly experienced symptoms at the beginning of the disease include a sudden onset of fever, intense weakness, muscle pain, headache, and a sore throat. As the disease progresses, other symptoms may develop, such as vomiting, diarrhea and jaundice (yellowness of the eyes). In severe cases, individuals may experience uncontrolled bleeding from body orifices and dysfunction or failure of several organs, including the kidneys, liver, and central nervous system. This can lead to shock and, ultimately, death. In fatal cases, death often occurs between 8 and 9 days after the onset of symptoms. Please contact NCDC for more enquiries or to report a suspected case on the toll-free number: 6232. Stay safe, Nigerians. item.title: 17 Years Later, Johnny Depp’s Overlooked Action Crime Thriller Is Officially Free on YouTube
item.description: Based on Bryan Burrough’s nonfiction book of the same name, Michael Mann’s Public Enemies puts Depp in the shoes of John Dillinger, one of the most prolific bank robbers in American history, set during his final few months of thieving in 1934. As he wreaks havoc across the Midwest, Dillenger attempts to stay one step ahead of Melvin Purvis (Christian Bale), a ruthless federal agent tasked with finally bringing him justice. With a proven track record of bringing crime epics to life, from Miami Vice to Heat , Mann captures a transformative moment when the relationship between criminals, the public, and the authorities was rapidly shifting. Dillinger became a symbol of defiance during the Great Depression, when banks were the furthest thing from beloved institutions, while the newly empowered FBI was working to establish itself as a formidable national force. The film’s historical scope is narrower than Burrough’s sprawling account of America’s crime wave, but that focus gives Mann room to explore the mythology surrounding one particularly charismatic outlaw.

item.title: The Opposition Has A Numbers Problem. Tinubu Has A Trust Problem
item.description: Nigeria’s presidential election is less than three months away, and something rather curious is happening. The ruling party is gathering supporters from almost every political direction. The opposition is gathering presidential candidates who cannot quite agree on who should lead them. And the electorate is being asked to choose between an administration defending difficult economic reforms and challengers promising a different future. There is plenty of political activity. What remains less clear is whether there is enough political persuasion. This Tuesday, three developments help explain where the race is heading: growing divisions within the opposition, a new controversy over the security of a presidential candidate, and an increasingly uncomfortable argument about who should bear the cost of Nigeria’s economic reforms. Together, they point to a contest that may ultimately be decided not by the size of political rallies, but by the credibility of the choices placed before Nigerians. 1. The opposition’s arithmetic is becoming complicated. (L-R) Kwankwaso and Atiku For months, the argument for a united opposition has seemed straightforward. If President Bola Tinubu’s opponents could combine their electoral strengths, they might present a formidable challenge to the APC. The difficulty, of course, is deciding whose name should appear at the top of the ticket. The latest reports suggest that this problem is becoming more pronounced. A coalition initiative involving several opposition parties is exploring the possibility of a common presidential candidate. But supporters of Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi are already disagreeing over who should lead such an arrangement. Rabiu Kwankwaso’s camp has also rejected suggestions that he should step aside for Atiku, while other presidential contenders continue to defend their ambitions. This is no longer merely a disagreement about personalities. It is a disagreement about the nature of the opposition itself. Should the objective be to assemble the largest possible coalition around the most experienced political operator? Or should it be to offer Nigerians a genuinely different political direction? Atiku’s supporters can argue that he has national networks, experience and an established electoral base. Obi’s supporters can point to his appeal among voters seeking a break from traditional politics. Kwankwaso’s political organisation offers another constituency that cannot simply be wished away. But there is an uncomfortable truth for all three camps. Votes are not bags of rice that politicians can simply transfer from one warehouse to another. A coalition agreement signed in Abuja does not guarantee that voters in Kano, Onitsha, Ibadan or Port Harcourt will follow the instructions of their preferred politicians. And the longer these negotiations continue, the less time remains for building the trust, campaign organisation and common policy programme needed to make a joint ticket credible. item.dc:creator: Emmanuel Egobiambu
item.content:encoded: Nigeria’s presidential election is less than three months away, and something rather curious is happening. The ruling party is gathering supporters from almost every political direction. The opposition is gathering presidential candidates who cannot quite agree on who should lead them. And the electorate is being asked to choose between an administration defending difficult economic reforms and challengers promising a different future. There is plenty of political activity. What remains less clear is whether there is enough political persuasion. This Tuesday, three developments help explain where the race is heading: growing divisions within the opposition, a new controversy over the security of a presidential candidate, and an increasingly uncomfortable argument about who should bear the cost of Nigeria’s economic reforms. Together, they point to a contest that may ultimately be decided not by the size of political rallies, but by the credibility of the choices placed before Nigerians. 1. The opposition’s arithmetic is becoming complicated. (L-R) Kwankwaso and Atiku For months, the argument for a united opposition has seemed straightforward. If President Bola Tinubu’s opponents could combine their electoral strengths, they might present a formidable challenge to the APC. The difficulty, of course, is deciding whose name should appear at the top of the ticket. The latest reports suggest that this problem is becoming more pronounced. A coalition initiative involving several opposition parties is exploring the possibility of a common presidential candidate. But supporters of Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi are already disagreeing over who should lead such an arrangement. Rabiu Kwankwaso’s camp has also rejected suggestions that he should step aside for Atiku, while other presidential contenders continue to defend their ambitions. This is no longer merely a disagreement about personalities. It is a disagreement about the nature of the opposition itself. Should the objective be to assemble the largest possible coalition around the most experienced political operator? Or should it be to offer Nigerians a genuinely different political direction? Atiku’s supporters can argue that he has national networks, experience and an established electoral base. Obi’s supporters can point to his appeal among voters seeking a break from traditional politics. Kwankwaso’s political organisation offers another constituency that cannot simply be wished away. But there is an uncomfortable truth for all three camps. Votes are not bags of rice that politicians can simply transfer from one warehouse to another. A coalition agreement signed in Abuja does not guarantee that voters in Kano, Onitsha, Ibadan or Port Harcourt will follow the instructions of their preferred politicians. And the longer these negotiations continue, the less time remains for building the trust, campaign organisation and common policy programme needed to make a joint ticket credible. The APC will be watching with considerable interest. Every week spent arguing about who should lead the opposition is a week the ruling party can spend campaigning. 2. Wike’s Rainbow Coalition meets resistance Wike (L) There is another coalition attracting attention, but this one is working in the President’s favour. Federal Capital Territory Minister Nyesom Wike has been promoting what he calls a Rainbow Coalition to support Tinubu’s re-election. The idea is politically attractive to the APC: recruit influential figures from other parties without necessarily requiring them to abandon their existing political platforms. But today’s reports suggest the arrangement is encountering resistance within the PDP. Party officials in Oyo, Imo, Edo and Bauchi, among other states, have distanced themselves from the initiative. Some insist that their party will continue to support its own candidates rather than subordinate its interests to Tinubu’s campaign. This matters for two reasons. First, it suggests that Wike’s political influence, although substantial, is not unlimited. Second, it raises an intriguing question about the future of party loyalty in Nigeria: Can a politician campaign for the presidential candidate of another party while remaining committed to his own party’s electoral success elsewhere? The answer may depend on political circumstances, but the implications go beyond Wike. If parties become vehicles for personal arrangements rather than institutions built around programmes and principles, the distinction between government and opposition becomes increasingly difficult for voters to understand. Tinubu may benefit from these arrangements in the short term. But the larger question is whether such alliances strengthen democratic competition or simply make it harder for citizens to identify who stands for what. 3. A dangerous allegation enters the campaign Atiku (centre) Today’s most troubling political development concerns an allegation about the safety of former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar. Timi Frank, a member of the ADC and former APC official, has alleged that there is a plot to assassinate the opposition presidential candidate. The APC Presidential Campaign Council has strongly denied the allegation. Its spokesperson, Dele Alake, challenged Frank to provide evidence and urged security agencies to investigate any credible threat. The council also stated that President Tinubu had directed security agencies to strengthen protection for candidates. There is no independently established evidence in the reporting reviewed that substantiates the alleged plot. Nevertheless, the development deserves attention. An election campaign should be a contest of ideas, personalities and political programmes, not an atmosphere in which threats and accusations dominate public discussion. If there is credible evidence of a threat, it must be investigated promptly and impartially. If an allegation is unfounded, that too should be established. Neither side should exploit such a serious matter for political advantage. The responsibility of the authorities is to ensure that every candidate can campaign freely and safely. That is not a favour to the opposition. It is a fundamental obligation of democratic government. 4. The economy returns to the centre of the campaign Organised labour has demanded a minimum wage review. Away from the coalition negotiations, another political confrontation is developing. The Nigeria Labour Congress has maintained its two-week ultimatum to the Federal Government, demanding renewed wage negotiations amid rising petrol prices and continued pressure on household incomes. Labour argues that the ₦70,000 minimum wage is no longer sufficient to meet basic living expenses. President Tinubu, meanwhile, has again defended the removal of petrol subsidies, insisting that he has no regrets about the decision. This is becoming one of the defining arguments of the 2027 election. The government says subsidy removal was necessary to correct longstanding economic distortions, reduce fiscal pressures and create the foundation for sustainable growth. Its critics argue that the immediate burden has fallen disproportionately on ordinary Nigerians. The question is no longer simply whether subsidy removal was economically justified. It is whether the government has done enough to protect those who have paid the highest price for the reform. The distinction is important. A policy can be economically defensible and still be politically damaging if its benefits remain distant while its costs are immediate. For Tinubu, the challenge is to convince Nigerians that the hardship associated with his reforms is producing measurable improvement. For the opposition, the challenge is equally demanding. It is easy to promise relief from high petrol prices. It is considerably harder to explain how that relief will be financed without recreating the fiscal problems that made subsidy reform necessary. item.title: MPs urge UK government to play venture capitalist with taxpayer-funded tech
item.description: Britain is funding the next generation of tech companies without making sure taxpayers get a slice of the action, MPs have warned. In a new report shared with The Register ahead of publication, the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) has accused UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) of being overly cautious about protecting taxpayers' interests. Rather than simply handing out grants, MPs want UKRI to consider taking equity stakes in more of the businesses it backs, giving the public a chance to cash in when those companies succeed. According to the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), UK universities produce more spinouts and patents per pound of research funding than their US counterparts. But Britain is less adept at cashing in on its inventions. British startups still struggle to attract the investment needed to grow without moving overseas, while universities have a patchy record when it comes to exploiting their intellectual property. UKRI, meanwhile, has been reluctant to impose tougher conditions on the research it funds, arguing that doing so could discourage companies from growing. “This approach is far too cautious and we urge the Department to do much more to recover taxpayer's money when a successful company exploits research which the taxpayer, via UKRI, has paid for," the PAC said. It wants UKRI to review its standard funding terms, including whether it should take equity stakes in more companies benefiting from public money. Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair of the PAC, acknowledged that calling for the government to behave more like a venture capitalist might seem an odd position for a committee normally concerned with keeping public spending in check. "It may strike followers of this Committee's work that our call for government to take a less cautious approach to taking a direct stake in British innovation is an unusual one," he said. "But we are a body dedicated to value for taxpayers' money, not hoarding it. item.dc:creator: Carly Page
item.content:encoded: Britain is funding the next generation of tech companies without making sure taxpayers get a slice of the action, MPs have warned. In a new report shared with The Register ahead of publication, the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) has accused UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) of being overly cautious about protecting taxpayers' interests. Rather than simply handing out grants, MPs want UKRI to consider taking equity stakes in more of the businesses it backs, giving the public a chance to cash in when those companies succeed. According to the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), UK universities produce more spinouts and patents per pound of research funding than their US counterparts. But Britain is less adept at cashing in on its inventions. British startups still struggle to attract the investment needed to grow without moving overseas, while universities have a patchy record when it comes to exploiting their intellectual property. UKRI, meanwhile, has been reluctant to impose tougher conditions on the research it funds, arguing that doing so could discourage companies from growing. “This approach is far too cautious and we urge the Department to do much more to recover taxpayer's money when a successful company exploits research which the taxpayer, via UKRI, has paid for," the PAC said. It wants UKRI to review its standard funding terms, including whether it should take equity stakes in more companies benefiting from public money. Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair of the PAC, acknowledged that calling for the government to behave more like a venture capitalist might seem an odd position for a committee normally concerned with keeping public spending in check. "It may strike followers of this Committee's work that our call for government to take a less cautious approach to taking a direct stake in British innovation is an unusual one," he said. "But we are a body dedicated to value for taxpayers' money, not hoarding it. The nations currently leading the global tech race did not achieve their positions by avoiding more entrepreneurial policies. This is a simple case for the government of nothing ventured, nothing gained." The government has made some effort to help British tech firms. UKRI gives AI startups free access to taxpayer-funded supercomputers, while DSIT has changed its procurement rules to give UK companies a better shot at supplying £400 million worth of specialist AI chips. The British Business Bank is also investing alongside pension funds, giving taxpayers a stake in some of the businesses receiving support. But efforts to attract more pension fund investment have been slower than ministers hoped, and MPs want DSIT to start measuring whether its various support schemes are actually helping British companies grow, rather than simply counting how much money it hands out. There's also the question of where all that research funding ends up. London, the South East, and the East of England continue to receive half of UKRI's funding, despite years of government promises to spread investment more evenly across the country. The North's share has improved from 12 to 20 percent over the past five years, but UKRI has yet to set specific regional funding targets. Clifton-Brown described the divide as "continuing and unacceptable," warning that progress could easily be reversed without a more deliberate effort to spread the cash around. And while MPs want UKRI to be more adventurous with its investments, they're considerably less impressed with how it manages some of the projects already on its books. The committee pointed to an airborne laboratory upgrade that UKRI abandoned after spending £46 million of its £49 million budget. Funding was finally canceled five years after the decision to upgrade the aircraft, prompting MPs to question why the plug hadn't been pulled sooner. Elsewhere, around 45 percent of the Science and Technology Facilities Council's estate is in unacceptable condition, and restoring university-owned research infrastructure to full working order would cost an estimated £5.6 billion. The PAC also criticized UKRI for failing to ensure a replacement for the ARCHER2 national supercomputer would be ready before the existing machine shuts down, leaving an expected 13-month gap. It seems Whitehall has mastered the art of spending money on innovation, but getting any back is another matter. ®

item.title: Sudanese Gold Miners Found ‘In Pieces’ After Egypt Border Airstrike
item.description: Days after an Egyptian strike killed scores of Sudanese gold miners on the border between the countries, wounded and traumatised survivors are trying to go back to the mines, with no other way to make a living. “I need to go get my gold,” 26-year-old Sharaf al-Din Ali told AFP, days after burying his friend with at least two dozen others in a shallow grave. He spoke from a waystation south of the border, where he was waiting for a truck to take him back to the mines of Jabal al-Uqaydat one last time. “Then I’m not coming back… But I can’t leave gold mining either.” Ali dropped out of college when war broke out between Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in April 2023. He is one of millions who have since flocked to the deadly gold trade, which fuels both sides of the conflict. Nearly all of it is routed through the United Arab Emirates, much of it first travelling through Egypt. Thousands had flocked to the sprawling, rugged mountains in the border area, where Ali Mohamed Hamdan, 29, was drinking tea with his fellow miners on October 10 when an aircraft began circling overhead. “It made three rounds, on the fourth it fired a missile,” he told AFP, lying in a cot in eastern Sudan after making it home with minor injuries. Sudanese rights group the Emergency Lawyers said at least 72 people were killed in the airstrike it blamed on the Egyptian military, which said it had conducted an operation targeting illegal miners “within its territory”. The family of Othman Omar Abdelrazik and Omar Abkar Abdelrazik, who were killed in airstrikes on a gold mine on the Sudan-Egypt border on October 11, receive condolences at their home in Wad al-Hulaywah, Kassala State in eastern Sudan on October 16, 2026. The number is widely considered a conservative figure, with hundreds of miners — many of them children — still unaccounted for in the rugged mountains. Eleven have been reported killed from Hamdan’s tiny hometown of Wad al-Hulaywah alone. In the farming village near the Ethiopian border, AFP met the handful of survivors who made it home, and the bereaved families whose sons never will. Village In Mourning Another survivor, Omar Mohieddin, said people had initially relaxed when the aircraft disappeared from view. “They came every day or two, so people were used to them,” he told AFP. “When it flew north, everyone thought it had gone.” But it returned minutes later, and he said he could see “the Egyptian flag on it”. At the first explosion, Hamdan and three others threw themselves into a hole, he said. When he emerged, one of his comrades’ “insides were outside his body”. The village has been in mourning for a week. Groups of men in white jellabas sit shoulder to shoulder, their faces drawn with exhaustion and shock. This month’s strike occurred in the vast, mineral-rich mountains between Sudan and Egypt, which include the Halayeb Triangle claimed by both countries and controlled by Egypt.
